options.metric: Annual number of reported motorist and cyclist deaths
options.reason: A direct count comparison is the clearest way to show how the two annual death totals move over time.
options.answer: Motorist deaths exceeded cyclist deaths in every year, ranging from 72 versus 18 in 2016 to 139 versus 29 in 2020.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how the annual death counts for the two road-user groups compare, with motorists higher in every year shown. Counts are a defensible direct comparison, but without travel or population exposure data they do not compare per-trip or per-person risk.

options.reason: The annual difference makes the size of the count gap between the groups immediately visible.
options.answer: Motorist deaths were higher in all 13 years; the gap ranged from 51 deaths in 2019 to 115 in 2021.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how many more motorist deaths than cyclist deaths were recorded each year, and all bars show a positive gap. Subtracting the two counts is a direct measure of their annual difference, but it does not describe exposure-adjusted risk or the pedestrian death count.

options.metric: Cyclist deaths as a percentage of motorist plus cyclist deaths
options.denominator: Motorist deaths plus cyclist deaths in the same year
options.reason: A share shows the relative balance between the two groups without being driven solely by the combined size of their counts.
options.answer: Cyclists accounted for between 9.1% of combined motorist-and-cyclist deaths in 2013 and 27.4% in 2019.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how the cyclist portion of deaths among these two groups changed year by year, with a low of 9.1% in 2013 and a high of 27.4% in 2019. This is a defensible relative comparison for these two categories, but it excludes pedestrian deaths and does not measure risk per unit of travel.
